slides.0.title: Regulations and labels
slides.0.subtitle: AOC, IGP, Vin de France and the Languedoc AOC rules
slides.1.title: Three tiers
slides.1.highlights.0.title: AOP / AOC
slides.1.highlights.0.content: Strictest: defined area, varieties, yields and methods
slides.1.highlights.1.title: IGP (Pays d'Oc etc.)
slides.1.highlights.1.content: Formerly Vin de Pays, with looser rules (Wikipedia); Pays d'Oc is over half the region by volume (Wine With Seth)
slides.1.highlights.2.title: Vin de France
slides.1.highlights.2.content: Replaced Vin de Table as the basic category; variety and vintage may generally be stated (after the 2009 EU reform)
slides.1.content: Languedoc holds both the strictest and the freest ends of the system.
slides.2.title: Languedoc AOC rules (2023 specification)
slides.2.highlights.0.title: Reds
slides.2.highlights.0.content: Always a blend: principal varieties (Grenache, Lledoner Pelut, Mourvèdre, Syrah) at least 50%; Mourvèdre plus Syrah at least 20%; Carignan and Cinsaut each capped at 40%; at least two varieties planted
slides.2.highlights.1.title: Whites
slides.2.highlights.1.content: Principal varieties include Bourboulenc, Clairette, Grenache Blanc, Marsanne, Piquepoul Blanc, Roussanne, Tourbat and Vermentino; Piquepoul Blanc capped at 50%, Viognier at 10%
slides.2.highlights.2.title: Yields and density
slides.2.highlights.2.content: Base yields: 50 hL/ha red, 54 rosé, 60 white; minimum planting density 4,000 vines/ha
slides.2.content: These are the rule-based facts exams like to test.
slides.3.title: The pyramid and naming
slides.3.highlights.0.title: The current pyramid
slides.3.highlights.0.content: AOP Languedoc and the DGCs form the base, sub-regional AOPs the middle and communal AOPs the top (Languedoc AOC page)
slides.3.highlights.1.title: Five communal AOPs
slides.3.highlights.1.content: Boutenac, Faugères, La Clape, La Livinière, Montpeyroux; Montpeyroux's standalone status is still pending and sources differ, so it is not tested
slides.3.highlights.2.title: 11 DGCs
slides.3.highlights.2.content: Such as Pézenas, Sommières, Grès de Montpellier, Saint-Saturnin (DGC = Dénomination Géographique Complémentaire, added after "Languedoc")
slides.3.content: The naming is intricate: remember that Languedoc is the base and communal appellations sit on top.
slides.4.title: Special cases and dates
slides.4.highlights.0.title: Picpoul de Pinet
slides.4.highlights.0.content: A white-only AOC, 100% Piquepoul Blanc; its own specification dates from a decree of 23 September 2013
slides.4.highlights.1.title: Limoux sparkling
slides.4.highlights.1.content: Blanquette de Limoux is first documented in 1531 at Saint-Hilaire Abbey, at least 90% Mauzac, traditional method; Crémant de Limoux became an AOC in 1990
slides.4.highlights.2.title: VDN
slides.4.highlights.2.content: Vin Doux Naturel: 5–10% grape spirit (min. 95% abv) added mid-fermentation; Roussillon makes about 80% of France's VDN
slides.4.content: Whether Fitou or Blanquette de Limoux was "the first appellation" is disputed in the sources, so it is not tested.
